human-medicines-regulations.definition: The main UK law on medicines. It says what a medicinal product is, who may sell or supply one, and which acts are crimes.

aliases: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
mhra.definition: The UK medicines regulator. It licenses medicines, runs the Yellow Card scheme and has its own unit that investigates crimes involving medicines.

unlicensed-medicine.definition: A medicine that has no licence (marketing authorisation) in the country where it is sold. Its safety, effect and quality have not been assessed there.

special-medicinal-product.definition: In the UK, an unlicensed medicine made or imported for one patient, ordered by a doctor or other prescriber for that patient's clinical needs.

misuse-of-drugs-act.definition: The UK law on controlled drugs. It sorts them into Class A, B and C, with criminal penalties for owning or supplying them.

class-c-drug.definition: The lowest of three groups of controlled drugs in the UK. It includes some hormones, such as growth hormone, but none of the peptides on this site.

conviction-on-indictment.definition: In the UK, a conviction after the more serious kind of criminal trial, usually in the Crown Court. Higher penalties are possible than in a magistrates' court.

ukad.definition: The national anti-doping organisation of the United Kingdom. It tests athletes and applies the World Anti-Doping Code in the UK.

usada.definition: The national anti-doping organisation of the United States. It tests athletes and applies the World Anti-Doping Code there.

fdca.term: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
fdca.definition: The main US federal law on medicines, foods and cosmetics. The FDA enforces it.

unapproved-new-drug.definition: In US law, a drug that experts do not generally recognise as safe and effective for its use, and that the FDA has not approved. It may not be sold across state lines.

interstate-commerce.definition: In US law, trade that crosses the border between two or more states. The federal ban on selling unapproved new drugs applies to it.

bulk-drug-substance.definition: The raw active ingredient, often a powder, from which a pharmacy or factory makes a medicine.

warning-letter.definition: A public letter from the FDA telling a company that it is breaking the law and must fix it. If it does not, the FDA can take further steps, such as seizing products.

drug-shortage-list.definition: The FDA's list of medicines that are in short supply in the US. While a medicine is on it, US law allows more compounding of copies.

federal-register.definition: The official daily journal of the US government. Proposed and final rules, and notices of FDA advisory meetings, are published there.

rulemaking.definition: How a US agency makes a binding rule: it publishes a proposed rule, takes public comments, and then publishes a final rule.

personal-importation.definition: Bringing a medicine into a country for your own use, in your luggage or by post, rather than to sell it.

right-to-try.definition: A US law of 2018. A person with a life-threatening illness can ask for a medicine that has finished a first human trial but is not approved. The FDA does not review the request, and the company does not have to agree.

eams.definition: A UK scheme that lets people with a life-threatening or seriously disabling condition get a medicine before it is licensed. A company must hold a scientific opinion from the MHRA and be able to supply it. Taking part is voluntary.

advisory-committee.definition: A group of outside experts that gives a regulator advice. Its vote is a recommendation, not a decision.

prohibited-list.definition: WADA's yearly list of substances and methods banned in sport. A new list takes effect each 1 January.

wada-s2.definition: The section of the WADA Prohibited List for peptide hormones, growth factors and similar substances. It names TB-500 and several growth-hormone peptides. They are banned at all times.

wada-s4.definition: The section of the WADA Prohibited List for substances that change hormones or metabolism. It names MOTS-c. They are banned at all times.

specified-substance.definition: In anti-doping rules, a banned substance that is more likely to have been taken for reasons other than sport. It is not less dangerous. The standard ban is shorter than for non-specified substances.

therapeutic-use-exemption.definition: Permission from an anti-doping organisation for an athlete to use a banned substance for a medical reason. Four strict tests must all be met.

global-dro.definition: A free website where athletes can check whether a medicine is banned in sport. It covers medicines sold in the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and a few other countries.

recreational-athlete.definition: Under the 2027 World Anti-Doping Code, an athlete below national level, as each national anti-doping organisation defines it. Lower bans are possible for them.

contaminated-source.definition: In anti-doping rules, a product or food with a banned substance that its label does not mention. It can lower a ban only in rare cases.

testing-pool.definition: A group of top athletes who must say where they are, so they can be tested without warning, also outside competitions.

ghrh.definition: A hormone from the brain that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. Lab-made versions such as tesamorelin and CJC-1295 copy it.

gh-secretagogue.definition: A substance that makes the body release more growth hormone, for example by acting like the hunger hormone ghrelin. Ipamorelin is one.

ghrp.definition: A small lab-made peptide that makes the body release growth hormone. Hexarelin is one.

ampk.definition: An enzyme inside cells that senses how much energy is available and switches energy use up or down.

unesco-convention.term: International Convention against Doping in Sport
unesco-convention.definition: A 2005 treaty by which governments agree to support the fight against doping. Its annex is the WADA Prohibited List.
